B13_00: Cell spreading and migration in tissues, concerning how cells hold back the formation of membrane folds at their leading edge when they should stay in place. This balance between moving and maintaining stable contacts matters for epithelial and immune cells. When the restraint is lost, cells can become inappropriately motile and invasive, a feature of tumour spread.
B13_01: Cellular self-digestion in nutrient-rich or stressed cells, focusing on the brakes that keep it from running unchecked. Balanced restraint matches basal turnover to demand; too little leads to excessive consumption of cell contents, while too much prevents removal of damaged mitochondria and aggregated material. That clearance failure is linked to neurodegeneration, notably familial Parkinson disease.
B13_02: Neural circuits of the brain and spinal cord, concerning how many inhibitory synapses form between neurons and how quickly. This sets the balance between excitation and inhibition that keeps circuits stable. Reduced inhibitory synapse numbers are associated with epilepsy and with neurodevelopmental disorders in which circuits become hyperexcitable, within developmental and activity-dependent circuit refinement.
B13_03: Dividing cells in proliferating tissues, where centrosome number must be held at two per cycle. Losing this control produces extra centrosomes, abnormal division and chromosome imbalance, a hallmark of tumours, which is why several factors involved behave as tumour suppressors, including one linked to hereditary breast and ovarian cancer. Defects also underlie microcephalic dwarfism syndromes.
B13_04: Nerve terminals in the brain, where synaptic vesicles must be readied for release. How many vesicles are ready sets release probability, short-term plasticity and the fidelity of fast synaptic transmission between neurons. Loss of this capacity causes severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathies and movement disorders in infants and children, making it central to normal brain function.
B13_05: The neuromuscular junction, where motor neurons meet skeletal muscle fibres and a specialised synapse must be built at the precise point of contact. Its proper assembly ensures reliable transmission from nerve to muscle during development and throughout life. Defects, whether inherited or caused by autoantibodies, produce congenital myasthenic syndromes and myasthenia gravis, with fatigable muscle weakness.
B13_06: Epithelial and endothelial barriers lining the gut, blood vessels and brain, concerning signals that loosen the seals between neighbouring cells and raise permeability. Such loosening is normal during wound repair, tissue remodelling and white blood cell passage, but when sustained it causes the leaky gut and blood-brain barrier of inflammatory disease, loss of epithelial organisation in invasive tumours, and vascular leakiness preceding metastasis.
B13_07: Muscle and other cells in which the length of fine cytoskeletal filaments must be fixed, including the contractile units of cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle, the red blood cell membrane skeleton and neurons. Uniform filament length is essential for muscle contraction and cell shape. Loss of the skeletal muscle form causes nemaline myopathy, and related defects disrupt contractile development.
B13_08: Motile and immune cells, where the growth of cytoskeletal networks controls how fast the cell edge protrudes, how quickly cells migrate and how the cell cortex is remodelled during adhesion and immune activation. It is clinically illustrated by an inherited immunodeficiency in which T cell activation and immune responses fail, leaving patients prone to recurrent infections.
B13_09: Migrating cells such as growing axons, endothelial cells forming new vessels, cells closing wounds and invasive tumour cells, concerning how they restrain their leading edge to stop, turn or hold still. This restraint shapes neural wiring, wound repair and angiogenesis. Its loss produces persistent, poorly directed movement, as when guidance fails during nervous system development or carcinoma cells become invasive.
B13_10: Neurons in the brain, concerning how quickly and extensively the receiving side of excitatory and inhibitory synapses is assembled on dendrites. This sets the number and shape of dendritic spines and therefore synaptic strength, learning and the balance of circuit excitability. Defects contribute to intellectual disability, autism and schizophrenia risk.
B13_11: Motile cells and especially developing neurons, concerning how the formation of thin exploratory projections is held back. In the cortex this restraint sets the pace of dendritic spine maturation and synapse formation; a human-specific gene duplication slows this pace and is linked to the prolonged spine development characteristic of the human brain. Loss of control gives excess projections and miswired connectivity.
B13_12: Innate immune cells such as macrophages and microglia facing infection, tissue injury or crystal deposits, concerning brakes that keep an inflammatory alarm from tipping into self-damaging inflammation. Without them, sterile or infectious triggers drive chronic disease, including periodic fever syndromes, gout, atherosclerosis and neuroinflammation. These brakes set the threshold for innate immune activation and inflammatory cell death.
B13_13: Dividing cells and especially neurons, where the cytoskeleton must be able to shrink as well as grow so that the division apparatus and axonal growth cones can remodel. In neurons this dynamic balance governs axon growth and regeneration after injury. Loss of such restraint contributes to axonal degeneration and is connected to synucleinopathies such as Parkinson disease.
B13_14: The developing and mature brain, concerning signals that limit how many synapses form between neurons. Restraining synapse formation refines circuits during development and keeps excitatory drive within bounds in adulthood. Loss of such restraint is associated with excess dendritic spine density, aberrant connectivity and epileptiform activity, representing the inhibitory side of synaptic connectivity and pruning.
B13_15: Membrane fusion inside cells, most importantly at nerve terminals, where it governs the readiness of vesicles for transmitter release, and in the system that delivers material to lysosomes for degradation. Neuronal defects cause severe infantile epilepsy and paroxysmal dyskinesia, and the process is linked to Parkinson disease, while the lysosomal arm connects to lysosomal disorders and neurodegeneration.
B13_16: Cells exposed to oxidative, heat or nutrient stress, which form temporary cytoplasmic granules that hold unused transcripts while protein production pauses. Readiness to form these granules buys time for repair and supports survival under energy stress. Persistent or abnormal granule formation is an entry point to pathological aggregation in neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia.
B13_17: General protein quality control in cells, concerning whether and how extensively proteins come together into functional complexes. Because the same tendency that builds working complexes also yields harmful aggregates, this control matters for the misfolded protein deposits that accumulate in neurodegenerative disease when clearance fails. It connects cellular housekeeping, internal sorting, and responses to stress and infection.
B13_18: Innate immune cells detecting infection by bacteria and viruses, or self material leaking from damaged host nuclei, concerning how readily an inflammatory alarm is raised. Raising it commits an infected cell to inflammatory signalling and pyroptotic death, so its tuning decides whether the cell is sacrificed or spared. Mistuning contributes to autoinflammatory tissue damage.
B13_19: Dividing cells in proliferating tissues, concerning how quickly and faithfully the division apparatus forms before chromosomes separate. Errors produce multipolar or misoriented divisions, lagging chromosomes and aneuploidy, which are hallmarks of cancer cells. Several of the factors involved are therefore studied as targets for anti-mitotic cancer drugs.
